slides: Okay, advanced circles. A quick summary before you practice.
The tools for the hardest circle questions, one at a time.
A shaded region? Don't calculate it directly. Build a scheme: which shape, minus which shape.
Say a square with an area of sixty-four, minus a quarter circle of sixteen pi. So the shaded part is sixty-four minus sixteen pi.
Overlapping circles? Split the region into pieces you know. Or add both, and take away the overlap.
The region between a chord and its arc... that's the sector, minus the triangle.
Radius four, angle sixty: the sector is eight pi over three. And the triangle is equilateral, so it's four root three.
Two equal circles, each through the other's center: you get two equilateral triangles, a hundred and twenty degrees, and two segments.
Three nested objects to know by heart. A square in a circle in a square, twice. Circle, square, circle, twice. And equilateral triangles, four times.
Anything else inside a circle? Write every length with r.
And careful. A length factor is not an area factor. Root two for lengths is two for areas.
Radii and tangents make right triangles all the time.
A leg that's half of the hypotenuse? That's the thirty, sixty, ninety triangle. Two equal legs? Forty-five, forty-five, ninety.
And two radii with a sixty-degree angle? An equilateral triangle.
A line touches two touching circles. So draw the radii to the line, join the centers, and cut off a right triangle.
With radii eighteen and two, that's two root thirty-six... twelve.
A chord of the big circle that touches the small one? The ring is pi times half the chord, squared.
Two arcs together, two sectors together... often you can't find each one. And you don't need to.
Four alpha and four beta make a full turn, so alpha plus beta is ninety. And that's all we need.
Letters in the question? Choose easy numbers, solve, and test the choices.
Estimate sizes to cross out choices. An area can't be negative. And a circle is smaller than the square around it.
And a ratio of two lengths can't have r in it.
Okay, before each question, ask yourself these.
And the common traps: treating a triangle as a right triangle when it isn't, taking the wrong fraction of the circle, and using a length factor for an area.
You know all of this. Now go practice.
